title: conditional two-locus genotype probability
stem: Two genes A/a and B/b are on different chromosomes. In an AaBb × AaBb cross, an offspring has both dominant phenotypes (A_B_). What is the probability that this offspring is AaBb?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1/4; the unconditional probability of AaBb is 1/4.
choices.rationale: This ignores the information that the offspring is already known to have both dominant phenotypes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 4/9; among the 9/16 offspring with both dominant phenotypes, 4/16 are AaBb.
choices.rationale: Correct: Independent segregation gives P(AaBb)=1/2×1/2=1/4=4/16 and P(A_B_)=3/4×3/4=9/16. Conditioning yields (4/16)/(9/16)=4/9.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 9/16; this is the probability of the observed phenotype, not the conditional genotype.
choices.rationale: This is the frequency of the conditioning phenotype rather than the requested genotype given that phenotype.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 1/9; each dominant phenotype forces a homozygous dominant genotype.
choices.rationale: Dominant phenotypes include both homozygotes and heterozygotes; they do not force homozygosity.

title: conditional two-locus genotype probability (variant 1)
stem: Genes A/a and B/b segregate independently. In an AaBb × Aabb cross, a randomly selected offspring has phenotype A_bb. What is the probability that the offspring genotype is Aabb?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1/2; half of all offspring are Aa before conditioning on the A_ phenotype.
choices.rationale: The unconditional Aa frequency must be divided by the 3/4 chance of A_.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1/4; this treats the A and B genotypes as two independent heterozygote probabilities after conditioning.
choices.rationale: The given recessive b phenotype fixes bb, so another factor of 1/2 should not be applied.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1/3; this counts the AA share among A_ offspring instead of the Aa share.
choices.rationale: Only one of the three dominant-A genotype parts is AA; two are Aa.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 2/3; among A_ offspring, two thirds are Aa, and bb is already specified.
choices.rationale: Correct: At A, Aa×Aa gives AA:Aa:aa=1:2:1, so P(Aa|A_)=2/3. At B, Bb×bb can yield bb, and the observed bb phenotype fixes that genotype. Thus P(Aabb|A_bb)=2/3.

title: conditional two-locus genotype probability (variant 2)
stem: Two independently assorting genes are crossed as AaBb × aaBb. An offspring has phenotype A_B_. What is the conditional probability that it is AaBb?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2/3; A_ forces Aa in this cross, while two of the three B_ genotype parts are Bb.
choices.rationale: Correct: At A, the aa parent contributes a, so an A_ offspring must be Aa. At B, Bb×Bb gives BB:Bb:bb=1:2:1, and P(Bb|B_)=2/3. Therefore P(AaBb|A_B_)=2/3.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1/2; this uses the unconditional probability of Bb.
choices.rationale: B_ is known, so its Bb probability is 2/3 rather than the unconditional 1/2.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1/3; this selects BB rather than Bb among B_ offspring.
choices.rationale: One third of B_ offspring are BB; the requested genotype has Bb.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 1/4; this multiplies two unconditional heterozygote probabilities.
choices.rationale: Conditioning makes A_ deterministically Aa here, so an extra 1/2 factor is wrong.

title: conditional two-locus genotype probability (variant 3)
stem: Two genes assort independently in an AaBb × AaBb cross. Among offspring that show both dominant phenotypes (A_B_), what fraction has genotype AABb?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1/8; this is the unconditional chance of AABb.
choices.rationale: The phenotype has been observed, so divide the unconditional genotype chance by 9/16.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 4/9; this is the conditional chance of AaBb, a different genotype.
choices.rationale: AaBb has twice as many heterozygote possibilities as the requested AABb genotype.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: P(AABb)=P(AA)P(Bb)=1/4×1/2=1/8=2/16. The observed A_B_ phenotype occurs 9/16 of the time, so P(AABb|A_B_)=2/9.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 1/9; this assumes that both dominant phenotypes force AA and BB.
choices.rationale: A dominant phenotype does not uniquely identify a homozygous dominant genotype.

title: testcross chi-square decision
stem: A dihybrid testcross for two genes on different chromosomes predicts four equally frequent phenotypes. Observed counts are 30, 20, 27, 23 (total 100). At α=0.05, the chi-square critical value with 3 degrees of freedom is 7.815. Which calculation and conclusion are justified?

choices.label: A
choices.text: χ²=7.815 by definition; the data prove that the genes assort independently.
choices.rationale: The critical value is a threshold, not a statistic computed from these observations; failure to reject cannot prove a model.

choices.label: B
choices.text: χ²=2.32, below 7.815; fail to reject the 1:1:1:1 null model.
choices.rationale: Correct: Expected count per class is 100/4=25. Sum (observed−25)²/25 over the four classes to get χ²=2.32. This is below the given 3-df critical value 7.815, so fail to reject the equal-classes null model; this test does not prove a particular biological cause.

choices.label: C
choices.text: χ²=2.32, below 7.815; reject the 1:1:1:1 null model.
choices.rationale: The numerical statistic is correct, but the decision direction is reversed relative to the critical value.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The four observed counts must be exactly equal or Mendel’s segregation law is disproved.
choices.rationale: Sampling variation can create unequal observed counts even when the 1:1:1:1 model is true.

title: pedigree two-child probability
stem: For a fully penetrant autosomal trait, two unaffected parents have an affected child. Assume no new mutation and independent outcomes for later births. What is the probability that, among their next two children, exactly one affected? Explain the parents’ inferred genotypes.

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1/4; only one birth needs to be considered despite the question asking about two.
choices.rationale: This uses a one-child probability or drops one of the possible two-child orders.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1/2; the affected child shows that one parent must be homozygous recessive.
choices.rationale: The parents are unaffected, so neither can be aa under complete penetrance; both are Aa.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 3/8; both parents must be heterozygous carriers (Aa × Aa), so each birth has a 1/4 affected chance.
choices.rationale: Correct: Unaffected parents of an affected aa child must both carry a: Aa×Aa. Each later child independently has P(affected)=1/4 and P(unaffected)=3/4. For exactly one affected among two children, the binomial/complement calculation gives 3/8.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 0; two unaffected parents cannot have a child with a recessive trait.
choices.rationale: Recessive inheritance allows unaffected carriers to have affected offspring.
